```{r setup}
#| include: false
library(lme4)
library(brms)
library(ggplot2)
col_teal <- "#1b6f8a"; col_red <- "#c0392b"; col_navy <- "#12384a"; col_muted <- "#9aa5ad"
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 13) + theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank()))
bayesplot::color_scheme_set("teal")
f2 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
pp  <- function(p) if (p > .995) "> .99" else paste("=", f2(p))
```

## What is brms?

[brms](https://paulbuerkner.com/brms/) is an R package for fitting **Bayesian regression models**, from simple linear models to complex multilevel models. You write the same formula syntax as in `lme4`, e.g. `y ~ x + (1 | id)`. brms translates the model into [Stan](https://mc-stan.org/), which estimates the posterior distribution of all parameters.

This makes brms an easy entry into Bayesian modelling for anyone who knows the models from *Linear Models in R*: the models stay the same, only the way of estimating them and of drawing conclusions changes.

## Topics

- Bayesian inference in a nutshell: prior, likelihood, posterior
- Choosing and checking priors (prior predictive checks)
- Fitting the course models in brms: linear models, GLMs, GLMMs
- Convergence diagnostics and posterior predictive checks
- Reporting: posterior summaries, credible intervals, predictions
- Link to [TAE](../tae/index.qmd): Bayes factors and the region of practical equivalence

::: {.key-terms}
**Key terms:** [Prior, posterior](../glossary.qmd#prior), [Credible interval](../glossary.qmd#credible-interval), [Rhat and effective sample size (ESS)](../glossary.qmd#rhat), [Divergent transitions](../glossary.qmd#divergent-transitions), [Convergence failure](../glossary.qmd#convergence)
:::

## Worked example: the Safe-vs-Risky box study

We return to the example from [session 11](../linear-models/sessions/11-glmm.qmd). Chimpanzees choose into which of two boxes a grape is dropped. The **Safe** box clearly guarantees delivery; in the **Risky** box, the grape seems to get stuck. In fact, both boxes always deliver.

- **RQ1:** Do chimps prefer the Safe box on trial 1?
- **RQ2:** Does this preference change over trials?

::: {.box-warn}
The study (with the MPI EVA, Leipzig) is preregistered, but the data do not exist yet. As in session 11, we use **simulated data of what we expect**: 15 chimps × 4 sessions × 10 trials, with an initial Safe preference (P = .70), no average change over trials, but chimps that differ in whether they drift towards Safe or Risky. So we know the true answer.
:::

### The data

```{r sim}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Simulation code (same as session 11)"
side_sequence <- function() {           # 5 x right, 5 x left; max. 2 in a row
  repeat {
    s <- sample(rep(0:1, 5))
    if (max(rle(s)$lengths) <= 2) return(s)
  }
}

sim_chimps <- function(n = 15, b0 = qlogis(0.70), b.trial = 0, b.side = 0.3,
                       sd.int = 0.8, sd.slope = 0.05) {
  ids <- sprintf("C%02d", 1:n)
  u0 <- setNames(rnorm(n, 0, sd.int), ids); u1 <- setNames(rnorm(n, 0, sd.slope), ids)
  d <- do.call(rbind, lapply(ids, function(id)
    data.frame(subject = id, session = rep(1:4, each = 10), trial = 1:40,
               side_safe = unlist(replicate(4, side_sequence(), simplify = FALSE)))))
  d$trial_c <- d$trial - 1                       # first-trial centred (as preregistered)
  eta <- b0 + u0[d$subject] + (b.trial + u1[d$subject]) * d$trial_c + b.side * d$side_safe
  d$safe <- rbinom(nrow(d), 1, plogis(eta))
  d
}

set.seed(120)
chimps <- sim_chimps()
```

```{r plot-data}
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-height: 3.4
by_sess <- aggregate(safe ~ subject + session, data = chimps, FUN = mean)
avg     <- aggregate(safe ~ session, data = chimps, FUN = mean)

ggplot(by_sess, aes(session, safe)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = .5, linetype = 2, colour = col_muted) +
  geom_line(aes(group = subject), colour = col_teal, alpha = .35) +
  geom_line(data = avg, colour = col_red, linewidth = 1.3) +
  geom_point(data = avg, colour = col_red, size = 2.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Session", y = "Safe choices",
       subtitle = "Thin lines: individual chimps · red: average")
```

### Step 1: the GLMM from session 11

```{r glmer}
glmm <- glmer(safe ~ trial_c + side_safe + (1 + trial_c | subject),
              family = binomial, data = chimps,
              control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))
```

```{r glmer-table}
#| echo: false
cf <- summary(glmm)$coefficients
ci <- confint(glmm, parm = "beta_", method = "Wald")
knitr::kable(data.frame(Estimate = f2(cf[, 1]), SE = f2(cf[, 2]),
                        `95% CI` = paste0("[", f2(ci[, 1]), ", ", f2(ci[, 2]), "]"),
                        p = formatC(cf[, 4], format = "f", digits = 3),
                        check.names = FALSE),
             align = "rrrr", caption = "Fixed effects (log-odds scale), Wald confidence intervals")
```

### Step 2: priors

A Bayesian model needs a prior for every parameter. We use **weakly informative priors** on the log-odds scale: they rule out absurd values but leave the data in charge.

```{r priors}
priors <- c(prior(normal(0, 1.5), class = "Intercept"),   # P(Safe) on trial 1
            prior(normal(0, 1),   class = "b"),           # trial and side effects
            prior(exponential(1), class = "sd"),          # between-chimp SDs
            prior(lkj(2),         class = "cor"))         # intercept-slope correlation
```

What do these priors imply *before* seeing any data? A **prior predictive check** translates them into chimp-level choice probabilities on trial 1:

```{r prior-pred}
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-height: 3
set.seed(1)
p_trial1 <- plogis(rnorm(1e4, 0, 1.5) + rnorm(1e4, 0, rexp(1e4, 1)))
ggplot(data.frame(p = p_trial1), aes(p)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = col_teal, colour = "white") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "P(Safe) on trial 1 for a chimp, implied by the priors", y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank())
```

The priors allow anything from a strong Risky to a strong Safe preference. They put somewhat more weight on extreme preferences than on 50%; a narrower intercept prior, e.g. `normal(0, 1)`, would flatten this.

### Step 3: fit the model

The formula is exactly the one from `glmer()`. `bernoulli` is the binomial family for single 0/1 choices.

```{r brm}
#| results: hide
fit <- brm(safe ~ trial_c + side_safe + (1 + trial_c | subject),
           family = bernoulli, data = chimps, prior = priors,
           chains = 4, iter = 2000, cores = 4, seed = 2026)
```

```{r brm-summary}
summary(fit)
```

All `Rhat` values are 1.00 and the effective sample sizes (`ESS`) are large, so the four chains agree. The trace plots should look like "hairy caterpillars", with no chain drifting off:

```{r trace}
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-height: 3.2
bayesplot::mcmc_trace(as.array(fit), pars = c("b_Intercept", "b_trial_c", "sd_subject__trial_c"),
                      facet_args = list(ncol = 3)) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

### Step 4: answer the research questions with the posterior

The posterior is a distribution, so we can answer the research questions **on the response scale and as probabilities**.

```{r posterior}
draws <- as_draws_df(fit)
# P(Safe) for an average chimp, averaged over the two sides
p1  <- plogis(draws$b_Intercept +                      0.5 * draws$b_side_safe)  # trial 1
p40 <- plogis(draws$b_Intercept + 39 * draws$b_trial_c + 0.5 * draws$b_side_safe)  # trial 40
```

```{r posterior-plot}
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-height: 3.2
post <- rbind(data.frame(trial = "Trial 1", p = p1), data.frame(trial = "Trial 40", p = p40))
ggplot(post, aes(p, fill = trial)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = .5, linetype = 2, colour = col_muted) +
  geom_density(alpha = .6, colour = NA) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(col_teal, col_red), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(.3, 1)) +
  labs(x = "P(Safe) for an average chimp", y = "Posterior density")
```

```{r rq-numbers}
#| echo: false
ci1 <- quantile(p1, c(.025, .975)); dd <- p40 - p1; cid <- quantile(dd, c(.025, .975))
```

- **RQ1:** On trial 1, an average chimp chooses the Safe box with probability `r f2(median(p1))`, 95% credible interval [`r f2(ci1[1])`, `r f2(ci1[2])`]. The posterior probability that chimps prefer the Safe box, i.e. that P(Safe) > .5, is `r sub("= ", "", pp(mean(p1 > .5)))`.
- **RQ2:** From trial 1 to trial 40, P(Safe) changes by `r f2(median(dd))`, 95% CrI [`r f2(cid[1])`, `r f2(cid[2])`]. The interval is wide: these data cannot rule out a moderate change in either direction. Whether the change is *practically zero* is a question for an equivalence test or a ROPE (see [TAE](../tae/index.qmd)).

The model-implied learning curve, with 95% credible band:

```{r cond-effects}
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-height: 3.2
ce <- conditional_effects(fit, effects = "trial_c")$trial_c
ggplot(ce, aes(trial_c + 1, estimate__)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = .5, linetype = 2, colour = col_muted) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower__, ymax = upper__), fill = col_teal, alpha = .25) +
  geom_line(colour = col_teal, linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Trial", y = "P(Safe)")
```

### Step 5: does the model reproduce the data?

A **posterior predictive check** simulates new datasets from the fitted model and compares them with the observed data. Here: the proportion of Safe choices for each chimp.

```{r ppc}
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-height: 4.2
pp_check(fit, type = "stat_grouped", stat = "mean", group = "subject", ndraws = 1000) +
  facet_wrap(~ group, ncol = 5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, .5, 1), labels = c("0", ".5", "1")) +
  labs(x = "Proportion of Safe choices") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The observed proportions (dark lines) lie well within the simulated ones for every chimp.

### Step 6: comparison with the GLMM from session 11

```{r compare}
#| code-fold: true
fe_b <- fixef(fit)
vc   <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(glmm))
sd_b <- summary(fit)$random$subject

tab <- data.frame(
  Parameter = c("Intercept (trial 1)", "Trial", "Side", "SD intercept", "SD trial slope", "Correlation"),
  True      = f2(c(qlogis(.7), 0, 0.3, 0.8, 0.05, 0)),
  glmer     = c(paste0(f2(cf[, 1]), " [", f2(ci[, 1]), ", ", f2(ci[, 2]), "]"),
                f2(vc$sdcor[1]), f2(vc$sdcor[2]), f2(vc$sdcor[3])),
  brms      = paste0(f2(c(fe_b[, 1], sd_b[, 1])), " [",
                     f2(c(fe_b[, 3], sd_b[, 3])), ", ", f2(c(fe_b[, 4], sd_b[, 4])), "]"))
knitr::kable(tab, align = "lrrr",
             col.names = c("Parameter", "True value", "glmer: estimate [95% CI]", "brms: mean [95% CrI]"),
             caption = "Log-odds scale. glmer reports no intervals for the variance components by default.")
```

```{r compare-plot}
#| code-fold: true
#| fig-height: 2.6
cmp <- data.frame(
  par   = rep(c("Intercept", "Trial", "Side"), 2),
  model = rep(c("glmer (session 11)", "brms"), each = 3),
  est   = c(cf[, 1], fe_b[, 1]),
  lo    = c(ci[, 1], fe_b[, 3]),
  hi    = c(ci[, 2], fe_b[, 4]))
cmp$par <- factor(cmp$par, levels = rev(c("Intercept", "Trial", "Side")))
truth   <- data.frame(par = factor(c("Intercept", "Trial", "Side"), levels = levels(cmp$par)),
                      est = c(qlogis(.7), 0, .3))

ggplot(cmp, aes(est, par, colour = model)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = col_muted) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), position = position_dodge(width = .5)) +
  geom_point(data = truth, aes(est, par), inherit.aes = FALSE, shape = 4, size = 3, colour = col_navy) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(col_teal, col_red), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Estimate (log-odds) with 95% interval; cross = true value", y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

**What stays the same, and what changes**

- **The estimates agree.** With weakly informative priors and 600 observations, the posterior means and credible intervals are very close to the `glmer()` estimates and confidence intervals. Bayesian modelling is not a different model, but a different way of estimating it.
- **The interpretation changes.** A 95% credible interval contains the parameter with 95% probability, given model and priors. That is how most people (mis)read a confidence interval anyway. And we can directly state things like "the probability that chimps prefer the Safe box on trial 1 is `r sub("= ", "", pp(mean(p1 > .5)))`".
- **Uncertainty about the variance components is visible.** `glmer()` gives only point estimates for the between-chimp SDs; brms gives full intervals. The wide interval for the SD of the intercept shows how little 15 chimps tell us about individual differences.
- **Complex random-effects structures become easier.** With only 15 individuals, `glmer()` often runs into convergence warnings or singular fits. The priors keep brms stable, which helps with the maximal random-effects structures recommended for confirmatory tests.
- **The price:** more computing time (here a few minutes instead of a second) and the need to choose and justify priors.

## Prerequisites

*Linear Models in R*. Please install brms and a Stan backend ([rstan](https://mc-stan.org/rstan/) or [cmdstanr](https://mc-stan.org/cmdstanr/)) before the workshop.
